senses.gloss:
crime and punishment
------------------------------------------
The problem of crime and the system of punishment have existed right from the days human beings began to live in organized societies. The contribution of Hindu jurisprudence in this regard, through its great saints like गौतम, आपस्तम्ब, बौधायन and Manu—all of whom lived centuries before the Christian era—and a galaxy of other writers right up to A.D. 1000 or more, is consider-able, both in quantity and quality.
One peculiar feature of this problem in India has been that social life and religious life being inextricably mixed up, it often becomes difficult to distinguish a crime from a sin or vice versa. Crimes should be punished but sins are to be expiated. All crimes are sins, but all sins are not crimes. Stealing is both a crime and a sin whereas neglect of his duties by a Vedic student is a sin but not a crime. A sin becomes a crime if it has social repercussions and impinges on the solidarity of the social system.
The धर्मशास्त्रस् (lawbooks guiding various aspects of socio-religious life of the Hindus) recognize the equality before law. None who committed a crime was exempt from punishment. Though details of punishments for various crimes have been meticulously worked out, the primary object was to protect the people of the society from the criminals and deter the potential criminals from committing such crimes.
Trials used to be conducted directly by the king himself or by the judges duly appointed by him. These judges had to be ब्राह्मणस् of unimpeachable character. However, though the judges could pronounce the sentence, it was for the king to execute the same.
The effect of the वर्ण-cum-चस्ते स्य्स्तेम् on punishments meted out for the same crime is clearly discernible in these writings. However, two diametrically opposite schools are met with. If some award more severe punishments to the members of the higher castes, since they ought to know better, others give less. The argument in the latter case is that being culturally more refined, they are psychologically more sensitive, and even lesser punishment will have the desired effect. After all, does not punishment entail a social stigma too? Even then, punishment awarded to the शूद्रस् for listening to the वेदस् or trying to learn them—which was considered to be a great offence—was extremely severe.
Whenever a criminal was punished, especially in the case of the higher caste groups, the offender was also to expiate himself through appropriate rites and discipline. This would render him fit for social intercourse later. If this was not done, more severe punishments would follow.
Cognizable offences listed in these lawbooks are legion: defamation, stealing, robbery, usurpation, sexual crimes of various types and degrees, treachery, physical assaults, murder, criminal abortion, offences against the State through espionage and sabotage, and so on.
Punishments were generally classified into four groups: vāgdaṇḍa (censure), dhigdaṇḍa (severe rebuke), dhanadaṇḍa (fines) and vadhadaṇḍa (corporal punishment). They could be awarded separately or jointly. The first two were for light offences only. Fines could be light or heavy, confiscation of property being the last word. However, even in such cases, the main tools and implements of workers, artisans, warriors, musicians etc., were not touched. The king was prohibited from appropriating the confiscated property to himself. Corporal punishment varied from simple flogging up to dismemberment of limbs or death. Punishments to women and old people or weaklings, were of lesser intensity. But, even ब्राह्मणस् and women were put to death if found guilty of heinous crimes. Offences of children below specified ages were not recognized. The sins of their wrongdoings were declared to go to their parents. Repeaters of crimes would invite more and more severe punishments. Public disgrace through ब्रन्दिन्ग् and shaving, or parading in the public streets was also resorted to, for certain crimes.
Viewing an offence as venial or mortal, varied from writer to writer or even according to times. Chronologically speaking, earlier lawgivers were more severe whereas the later ones were more lenient.
See PĀTAKA and PRĀYAŚCITTA also.
